info.bio:
Frankie Goes to Hollywood fue un grupo techno pop inglés, formado en Liverpool, a principio de los años 1980. Consiguieron notable éxito en el Reino Unido y en otros países con la canción Relax, con letras que aludían explícitamente a la homosexualidad.

Su formación originaria incluía Holly Johnson como vocalista, Paul Rutherford, los primos Mark y Jed O'Toole respectivamente al bajo y a la guitarra, Peter Gill a la batería. La banda se disolvió bastante pronto

own_scenes.desc: Veteranos de la escena glam punk del Eric's (Holly Johnson de Big in Japan, Paul Rutherford de los Spitfire Boys) más «the lads», con imagen sadomasoquista y homosexualidad declarada: los «Disco Pistols». Atrapados en un contrato humillante con ZTT, Horn graba «Relax» (1983) casi sin ellos, a ritmo de Hi-NRG con Fairlight y Linn sincronizados; la prohibición de la BBC la lleva al número uno. Morley planea una trilogía sobre sexo, guerra y religión: «Two Tribes» (nueve semanas en el número uno, con camisetas «FRANKIE SAY»), «The Power of Love». Welcome to the Pleasuredome decepciona, Estados Unidos los ve como unos Village People y acaban sin fans de verdad: anuncio del regreso de las boy bands. «¿No tuvieron alguna vez la sensación de que los engañaron?»

refs.q: Horn vio a Frankie Goes to Hollywood por primera vez en un nuevo programa de televisión inglés llamado The Tube
refs.para: Horn vio a Frankie Goes to Hollywood por primera vez en un nuevo programa de televisión inglés llamado The Tube. Esta banda de Liverpool había recibido un presupuesto acotado para filmar una versión más limpia del sórdido videoclip promociona! de "Relax", que los integrantes habían grabado para atraer la atención de las discográficas. El look del grupo era muy llamativo. Por ejemplo, Holly Johnson (el cantante) y Paul Rutherford (corista y tecladista) vestían ropa de cuero de corte claramente fetichista. El sonido, por otro lado, era funk rock desprolijo, crudo, enérgico. "Parece más un jingle que una canción", señaló Horn acerca de "Relax", pero también es cierto que él prefería los temas incompletos por sobre aquellos a los que no les faltaba nada, porque le permitían "mejorarlos", agregarles su estilo inimitable. A Morley, quien tenía sus dudas sobre la banda en un comienzo, le gustaba que exhibieran su homosexualidad. "Pensé que podría ser justo lo que estaba buscando, la oportunidad de inventar un grupo pop de cero." Sin embargo, Frankie Goes to Hollywood ya tenía una identidad propia. Antes de unirse a ZTT, la banda cultivaba una imagen sadomasoquista, un sonido extraño -mezcla de metal con música disco- y una gran fuerza de voluntad y perseverancia, como se deja ver en la expresión local "Give it loads!" [¡Denlo todo!], que se convirtió en el eslogan del grupo.
refs.chapter: Cap. 22: Tomar por asalto el siglo XX: ZTT, The Art of Noise y Frankie Goes to Hollywood

refs.para: "Relax" sonaba colosal, lo que no debería sorprender a nadie, considerando las setenta mil libras que costó su grabación. Aun así, Horn afirmó que la grandeza del sonido se debía menos a los trucos de producción que al tono del tema y a la instrumentalización que se empleó. '"Relax' es perfecta porque está en Mi", observó. "La nota más gratificante que emite el bajo es la cuarta cuerda tocada al aire, Mi, y es lo que se oye a lo largo de la canción". La tecnología también fue crucial, sin embargo. Gracias a un nuevo dispositivo, Horn pudo sincronizar el pulso de bajo del Fairlight con la caja de ritmos Linn a un nivel de perfección sobrehumano. La base rítmica del tema era impresionante, erótica. En su autobiografía, Johnson describe cómo "Relax" fusionaba "la agresividad del rock" con la música disco Hi-NRG tan difundida en los clubes gays a principios de los ochenta. El DJ y productor lan Levine, pionero del género, describió el Hi-NRG como "música dance melódica y simple, sin demasiado funk"; y esa falta de funk resultó vital. Los bajistas incluso resaltaban el beat más tosco y con poco swing de este tipo de música europea blanca poniendo mayor énfasis en la última nota de cada compás, nota que en la pista de baile se marcaba con un movimiento brusco de caderas.
refs.chapter: Cap. 22: Tomar por asalto el siglo XX: ZTT, The Art of Noise y Frankie Goes to Hollywood

refs.q: Frankie Goes to Hollywood se había convertido en el grupo inglés más exitoso de los ochenta
refs.para: "Two Tribes" ingresó a los rankings británicos en el puesto número uno el 4 de junio de 1984, donde permaneció durante nueve semanas, con la ayuda de una serie innumerable de remixes. Por su parte, "Relax" volvió a ascender al puesto número dos durante una semana. Frankie Goes to Hollywood se había convertido en el grupo inglés más exitoso de los ochenta: "Relax" era el cuarto single más vendido en la historia del Reino Unido hasta ese momento, y "Two Tribes", el undécimo, lo que representaba una justificación absoluta de las políticas de manipulación mediática de ZTT. "Es tonto, pero en cierto sentido la fantasía que tenía sobre el new pop en NME se volvió realidad gracias a mí", afirmó Morley. "En términos narrativos, era algo de una pureza casi sublime."
refs.chapter: Cap. 22: Tomar por asalto el siglo XX: ZTT, The Art of Noise y Frankie Goes to Hollywood

refs.q: En cierto sentido, Frankie Goes to Hollywood puede verse como el último eslabón en la cadena de la revolución punk
refs.para: En cierto sentido, Frankie Goes to Hollywood puede verse como el último eslabón en la cadena de la revolución punk; sin embargo, a un nivel más profundo o estructural, la banda era una muestra de lo que deparaba el futuro del pop: el regreso de las boy bands. Tak vez eso explique la extraña vacuidad del fenómeno que significó este grupo, aun durante el punto álgido de la frankiemanía. Al final, tanto los consumidores (quienes tuvieron que contentarse con la exuberancia insatisfactoria de Welcome to the Pleasuredome) como la banda (cuyos integrantes apenas recibieron unas pocas regalías con el correr de los años y debieron cargar con la humillante reputación de ser meros títeres en las manos de ZTT) bien podrían haber repetido la famosa frase de Lydon que dio la vuelta al mundo: "¿No tuvieron alguna vez la semación de que los engañaron?':

podcast.title: Origins at Eric's Club (1980)
podcast.body: The band's beginnings trace back to 1980 in Liverpool, where most of the members were regulars at a club called Eric's. This venue served as a formative hub for the group before their rise to fame. "The beginnings of the band go back to 1980 and the frontman was Holly Johnson."

podcast.title: Breakup and Internal Strife (1987)
podcast.body: The band officially broke up in 1987 after the release of their second album, "Liverpool," due to waning public interest and severe internal conflicts, including a backstage fistfight between singer Holly Johnson and bass player Mark O'Toole at a Wembley show in January. "The band broke up in 1987 following the release of their second album called Liverpool. They had basically worn out their welcome with the public, and things weren't going well internally."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 3

podcast.title: Final British TV Appearance (1987)
podcast.body: The original lineup of Frankie Goes to Hollywood made its final appearance on British television on March 21, 1987, after which everything dissolved into a complex series of lawsuits. "There was a final appearance on British TV on March 21, 1987. And that was it for the original Frankie goes to Hollywood."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 3

podcast.title: VH1's "Bands Reunited" (2003)
podcast.body: In 2003, all members were asked to appear on the VH1 show "Bands Reunited." Holly Johnson participated only through an interview, refusing to perform or engage in any subsequent revival efforts. "Everyone was asked to appear on that VH1 show called Bands Reunited. Holly did not want any part of the TV show or any subsequent revival, but he did appear on the show just the same, just an interview, though, no performance."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 3

podcast.title: Holly Johnson's Failed Trademark Attempt (2007)
podcast.body: To prevent other members from using the band's name without him, Holly Johnson attempted to register "Frankie Goes to Hollywood" as his personal trademark, but a judge ruled against him on June 7, 2007, deeming his attempt frivolous and ordering him to pay approximately 3,200 pounds in court costs. "Holly tried to register the name, Frankie goes to Hollywood as a trademark owned by him, thereby denying everything else to things like the name for gigs and t-shirts and CDs and DVDs, everything."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 3

podcast.title: Reunion with New Singer Ryan Maloy (2007)
podcast.body: The judge's ruling against Holly Johnson's trademark attempt opened the door for a Frankie Goes to Hollywood revival, which featured a new singer named Ryan Maloy. "That opened the door to the Frankie Revival, featuring a new singer named Ryan Maloy, and Holly had to pay about 3,200 pounds in court costs."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 3

podcast.title: All-Gay Lineup (Claimed)
podcast.body: It is rumored, though somewhat "murky" and possibly part of the band's "pure hype," that every member of Frankie Goes to Hollywood was gay. This claim contributed to their controversial and provocative image. "It's a bit murky, but it is said that every member of the band was gay."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Early Days of LGBTQ Rock

podcast.title: Attempt to Replace Singer Holly Johnson
podcast.body: Following internal strife, Liverpool singer Pete Wylie was secretly approached and asked if he would like to replace Holly Johnson as the band's new singer, but Wylie declined the offer. "Then a Liverpool singer named Pete Wiley was secretly called. The call went something like this. Hey, you know what? We're sick of Holly. Would you like to be our new singer? But Pete said, no, I don't want anything to do with this."

podcast.title: Fairlight CMI Usage (Year not specified)
podcast.body: The producer Trevor Horn utilized the Fairlight CMI, a complex digital sampler, for acts like Frankie Goes to Hollywood. This technology enabled innovative sound production, contributing to the distinct sound of their music. "Producer Trevor Horn bought a Fairlight and used it for acts like Frank Gusto Hollywood in the art of noise."

podcast.title: Fairlight Keyboard Use
podcast.body: Frankie Goes to Hollywood utilized the Fairlight, a sophisticated keyboard device that allowed for the digital excision, manipulation, and implantation of musical material, in the creation of their remixes during the 1980s. "Frankie and New Order used a Fairlight for their remixes."

podcast.title: New Name for Frankie Goes to Hollywood
podcast.body: This name was adopted by the former members of Frankie Goes to Hollywood to avoid further legal issues after Holly Johnson's failed attempt to trademark the original band name. "Well, working under the name for Bidden Holly Wood to avoid further legal issues."

podcast.title: Operating as Forbidden Hollywood
podcast.body: To avoid further legal complications and issues related to the band's name, the reconstituted group began working under the name "Forbidden Hollywood." "Well, working under the name for Bidden Holly Wood to avoid further legal issues."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 3

podcast.title: Pioneers of Remix Sales Strategy
podcast.body: Frankie Goes to Hollywood was exceptionally skilled at using remixes to drive sales in the early 1980s. From 1984 to 1987, they released only seven singles, but these were extensively remixed and re-released, resulting in three dozen different remix versions. This strategy provided "very low overhead, big profits" for the band and their label. "Frankie goes to Hollywood was really good at the remix trick. Between 1984 and 1987, Frankie released just seven singles. But those singles were remixed and re-released again and again and again. Those seven singles stretched into three dozen remixes."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Remixes

podcast.title: Post-Breakup Solo Efforts and Lawsuits
podcast.body: Following their breakup, members engaged in solo projects and spin-offs, but these endeavors largely failed to achieve significant success, while the band's dissolution escalated into numerous complicated lawsuits. "Everything dissolved into a series of lawsuits that are too complicated and boring to get into here."

podcast.title: Reunion Gap - 20 Years, Two Months, 18 Days
podcast.body: The original group split on March 21, 1987, and was officially allowed to reconstitute, albeit with a different lead singer, on June 7, 2007, marking an interval of 20 years, two months, and 18 days. "The group splits on March 21st, 1987 and was allowed to reconstitute, well, with other lead singer anyway, on June 7th, 2007. That's an interval of 20 years, two months, and 18 days."

xref.title: Impact of Bowie's "Coming Out"
xref.body: Holly Johnson of Frankie Goes to Hollywood credited David Bowie's "coming out" statement in January 1972 as having changed his life. Bowie's public bravery gave Johnson the courage to be who he was. "Boy George of Culture Club and Holly Johnson of Frankie Ghost of Hollywood say that their lives were changed by Bowie's comments."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Inspiration for LGBTQ+ Individuals
xref.body: Bowie's public comments about his sexuality in 1972 struck a chord with thousands who were afraid to come out, giving them courage and a sense of shared identity with a famous figure. Figures like Boy George of Culture Club and Holly Johnson of Frankie Goes to Hollywood have stated that Bowie's comments changed their lives. "Bowie gave them the courage to be who they were."

xref.title: Out Gay Frontman
xref.body: Holly Johnson, the frontman for Frankie Goes to Hollywood, was an openly gay man. His real name was William, but he adopted the name Holly in high school, inspired by the transvestite Holly Woodlawn, who was famously mentioned in Lou Reed's song "Walk on the Wild Side." "Holly Johnson, an out-game man whose real name was William."

xref.title: Snare Drum Sample for Frankie Goes to Hollywood
xref.body: A snare drum sound from a Led Zeppelin record was sampled and used in Frankie Goes to Hollywood's 1984 song "Relax." The original drum hit in the studio triggered this pre-manipulated sample. "The original sound comes from a Led Zeppelin record."
